# Notes on 1 Kings 3 (verse by verse)

**About these notes:** I didn't find tradition-specific sources on this chapter from LCMS, Wesleyan, Pentecostal (AG/Pneuma Review), Orthodox (OCA) or prosperity/word-of-faith writers, so those views are missing. The debates I did find are between individual commentators, not between denominations. I haven't added tradition labels where the pages don't give them.

---

**v. 1 (the marriage to Pharaoh's daughter)**
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Royal marriages were a normal way to seal treaties. He sees this one as the start of a bad pattern that foreign wives later used to turn Solomon's heart from God. He also notes it wasn't Solomon's first marriage: Rehoboam was born before it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
- **Guzik:** Marrying a foreigner wasn't against Moses' law if she converted. But he calls this marriage politically sensible and spiritually unwise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
- **A different view (Pulpit Commentary):** The Law only banned marriage with the nations of Canaan. Solomon is never blamed for this marriage, and there's no sign of Egyptian religion entering Israel, so the princess probably adopted Israel's faith. Pulpit adds that the alliance must have startled most Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Pulpit:** It's impossible to say for sure which Pharaoh this was. He was probably a late king of Egypt's 21st dynasty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html

**v. 2 (sacrifice on the high places)**
- **Guzik:** Before the temple, altars on high places were allowed as long as they were for the LORD and free of idolatry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
- **Clarke:** Sacrifice was lawful wherever the ark and tabernacle were. The tabernacle was then at Gibeon (2 Chronicles 1:3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-3.html
- **Pulpit (citing Keil):** Just as Solomon had to house his wife in the City of David because his palace wasn't finished, the people had to use high places because the temple wasn't built. Pulpit notes the people are never blamed for this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Grant (stricter view):** The high places were idolatrous shrines, and mixing them with the worship of God could not have God's approval. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/1-kings-3.html

**v. 3 ("loved the LORD… except")**
- **Guzik:** The verse holds both good and bad. Solomon generally walked in David's ways, but the bad lies in the word "except." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
- **Matthew Henry:** David stayed with the ark, while Solomon fell short of him on the high places. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_003.cfm
- **The commentators disagree here:**
  - Pulpit says high-place worship was tolerated, even accepted, but wasn't strictly right; God overlooked it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
  - Coffman warns against going easy on Solomon's sins. Against Jamieson, who said "only" carries no criticism, Coffman says it can mean nothing else. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-3.html
  - Precept Austin notes that "high places" is plural and finds no provision allowing several of them, so it concludes Solomon's practice was not proper. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-3-commentary
- **Pulpit (sermon section):** The best thing said of Solomon is not his wisdom or his wealth but that he loved the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html

**v. 4 (Gibeon and the thousand offerings)**
- **Why Gibeon was "great":** The tabernacle was there, even though the ark was in Jerusalem (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/ BibleHub's study notes say this makes Solomon's visit faithfulness to God's interim arrangement, not mixing in other religions. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/3-4.htm
- **Guzik:** The huge number of offerings showed both Solomon's wealth and his wish to use it for God's glory. The event marked the ceremonial start of his reign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
- **Pulpit:**
  - Solomon "offered" them in the sense that he supplied them; he didn't kill a thousand animals himself.
  - The feast probably lasted seven or eight days.
  - Gibeon is today's El-Jib, about six miles north of Jerusalem.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Constable:** Burnt offerings stood for the worshipper giving himself to God, so a thousand of them expressed Solomon's personal loyalty to the LORD. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-3.html

**v. 5 (the dream and God's offer)**
- **Pulpit:** God may have shown himself in some form, but the point is that he revealed himself. The night was probably the one after the last day of sacrifices. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Pulpit (homiletic section):** God appearing to Solomon at Gibeon shows his sacrifice there wasn't condemned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Guzik:** God's offer wasn't a reward for the thousand animals. It came because Solomon's heart was surrendered to God. Guzik links it to Christian promises about prayer (Matthew 7:7; John 15:7; 1 John 5:14). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/

**v. 6 (remembering God's kindness to David)**
- **Guzik:** Before asking for anything, Solomon remembered God's faithfulness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
- **Pulpit:** David himself had seen a son on his throne as a special mercy (1 Kings 1:48). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html

**v. 7 ("a little child")**
- **Guzik (citing Dilday):** This is poetic language for feeling inadequate, not his real age. It is humility that relies on God, not false humility that refuses to try. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
- **Pulpit:** The words show humility more than age, though it doubts a young man of about 20 would put it this way. "Go out or come in" is a standard phrase for how a person conducts his life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html

**v. 8 (a people too many to count)**
- **Pulpit:** The wording echoes God's promises to Abraham (Genesis 13:16; 15:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html

**v. 9 (an "understanding heart")**
- **The Hebrew word:** It means "hearing." Guzik reads it as a heart that listens to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/ Pulpit disagrees: it means sharp judicial insight, not teachability. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Pray for wisdom (James 1:5) aimed at your own calling. Solomon wanted it to judge the people, not to satisfy curiosity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_003.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** "Who is able…?" suggests only God can truly judge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-3-commentary
- **The Gospel Coalition (Reformed):** The request is more than selflessness. As David's son, Solomon is asking for the wisdom to build God's temple, a theme rooted in earlier Scripture. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/solomon-ask-wisdom/

**v. 10 (God was pleased)**
- **Guzik:** God was pleased by what Solomon asked for and by what he didn't ask for. Quoting Maclaren, he wonders whether David's deep longing for communion with God would have been even better. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
- **Pulpit:** Even in a dream, judgment and will were working; this would have been Solomon's choice at any time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html

**v. 11 (what Solomon didn't ask for)**
- **Pulpit:** "Death for your enemies" means military enemies more than personal ones. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **TGC devotional:** God praises Solomon for asking for nothing selfish or vengeful, but for skill in administering justice. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/1-kings-3-ephesians-1-ezekiel-34-psalms-83-84/
- **BibleHub Q&A:** "A heart that hears" echoes Deuteronomy's rules for judges and kings (Deut 1 and 17). https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_God_give_Solomon_wisdom.htm

**v. 12 (a wise heart, unmatched)**
- **Pulpit:** The comparison doesn't need to be limited to kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship):** With this divine decree, Solomon the legend was fixed in history. The article also says Chronicles retells Solomon's story but glosses over his less flattering traits. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/solomon/

**v. 13 (riches and honor too: the prosperity question)**
- I found no prosperity or word-of-faith source on this verse. The sources I found read it this way:
  - **Guzik:** God answered beyond what was asked (Ephesians 3:20). What we are matters more than what we have. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/
  - **Matthew Henry (via StudyLight):** The way to receive earthly blessings is to be indifferent to them. Solomon got wisdom because he asked for it, and wealth because he didn't. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/3-13.html
  - **G. Campbell Morgan (via Precept Austin):** Wealth chosen for selfish reasons would have been a curse. It blessed Solomon's people only while he sought the highest things. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-3-commentary
  - **Several sources** link the verse to Matthew 6:33 ("seek first the kingdom"). https://biblehub.com/1_kings/3-10.htm

**v. 14 (the condition for long life)**
- **TGC devotional:** Wisdom alone wasn't enough for Solomon to stay faithful; long life depended on obedience. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/1-kings-3-ephesians-1-ezekiel-34-psalms-83-84/
- **Pulpit:** Solomon probably died at about sixty or younger, so the promise of long life wasn't strikingly fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html

**v. 15 (waking, worship in Jerusalem, the feast)**
- **Pulpit:** This was a dream that carried a revelation, like Pharaoh's and Joseph's. The peace offerings gave thanks, and the feast was a sacrificial meal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Solomon gave thanks before the ark, as if blaming himself for not having prayed there. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_003.cfm
- **Grant:** The proper place for offerings was before the ark, not on high places. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/1-kings-3.html
- **Guzik, quoting Clarke:** Solomon later wasted these gifts. Clarke says no Bible character disappoints more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-3/

**v. 16 (two prostitutes before the king)**
- **What the word means:**
  - Some read *zonot* as "innkeepers" (Wiseman, quoted by Guzik). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-kings/1-kings-3.cfm
  - The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge prefers the Aramaic Targum's "tavern-keepers." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/1-kings/3-16.html
  - Pulpit says Jewish writers read it as "hostess" here, as with Rahab. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/3-16.htm
- **The majority reading is prostitutes, and the point is that justice reached the lowest people:**
  - Few kings would bother with such a case (Guzik). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-kings/1-kings-3.cfm
  - Constable and Precept Austin make the same point. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/3-25.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-3-commentary
- **Matthew Henry:** The case may already have stumped lower courts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/3-25.html

**vv. 17–18 (the first woman's story)**
- **Matthew Henry:** The women were so poor they had no nurse with them, and so shunned that no friends came with them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/3-25.html
- **Precept Austin:** No witnesses existed, which tested Solomon's gift. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-3-commentary

**vv. 19–21 (the death and the swap)**
- **Matthew Henry:** Infancy is "the valley of the shadow of death." He adds that these mothers still loved and nursed their children. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/3-25.html

**vv. 22–23 (the argument; Solomon sums up)**
- **Matthew Henry:** Solomon patiently heard both sides and summed up the evidence. Torturing the parties for evidence would have been barbaric and unreliable. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_003.cfm

**v. 24 ("Bring me a sword")**
- **Guzik:** The solution looked foolish at first, just as God's judgments can seem strange before time proves them wise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-kings/1-kings-3.cfm
- **Iain Provan (via Precept Austin):** In chapter 2 Solomon's sword carried out executions of questionable justice. Here it serves justice for the whole kingdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-3-commentary
- **BibleHub study notes:** These link the sword to Hebrews 4:12 and Revelation 19:15 (a picture of Christ's judgment). https://biblehub.com/1_kings/3-24.htm

**v. 25 ("Cut the living child in two")**
- **Gotquestions:** The text makes clear the aim was to find the truth, not to kill the child. https://www.gotquestions.org/Solomon-two-prostitutes.html
- **Was this supernatural wisdom? The commentators disagree:**
  - Clarke calls it sound judgment and knowledge of human nature, but "surely" not proof of extraordinary, supernatural wisdom.
  - Constable calls insight into human nature a gift from God and part of wisdom.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/3-25.html
- **Ellicott:** It was an intuitive appeal to a mother's instinct. It could have failed, but it was the only appeal possible. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/3-16.htm

**v. 26 (the true mother gives way)**
- **BibleHub study notes:** The test didn't create the women's characters; it revealed them. Envy made the false woman prefer the child dead. https://biblehub.com/study/1_kings/3-26.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** By agreeing, the false mother showed she knew her claim was bad. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/3-25.html
- **Pulpit:** It suggests Hebrews 4:12 may have had this scene in mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-3.html
- **Catholic/patristic view:** Jerome (Letter 74, AD 398) treats the story as a parable, with the false and true mothers standing for the Synagogue and the Church. I could only read New Advent's summary, not the letter itself. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001074.htm

**v. 27 (the ruling)**
- **Gotquestions:** Solomon identified the mother from how the two women responded. https://www.gotquestions.org/Solomon-two-prostitutes.html

**v. 28 (Israel in awe)**
- **Gotquestions:** The case showed Solomon really had received wisdom from God. https://www.gotquestions.org/Solomon-two-prostitutes.html
- **Bridgeway (via StudyLight):** Solomon didn't let the women's low morals affect his sense of justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/3-25.html
- **Bible Odyssey:** It calls the verdict the classic example of Solomon's "wise and discerning mind." https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/solomon/
